bib.title: Common Voice: A Massively-Multilingual Speech Corpus

question: Can a crowdsourced, permissively licensed, multilingual speech corpus be built, and does it support end-to-end ASR research in low-resource languages?
hypothesis: Transferring layers from a pre-trained English DeepSpeech model improves character error rate on target languages.
contributions: Common Voice: crowdsourced multilingual speech corpus released under CC0
Recording and validation pipeline using contributor votes
Speaker-disjoint splits sized by statistical power analysis
Transfer-learning ASR experiments on 12 languages with DeepSpeech

method.summary: Contributors read prompted sentences; other contributors vote clips valid or invalid. Speaker-disjoint train/dev/test splits are made. DeepSpeech v0.3.0 is fine-tuned from an English model with 0 to 5 layers copied, per target language, and scored by CER.
method.task: multilingual end-to-end ASR (corpus construction plus transfer-learning experiment)

datasets.name: Common Voice (June 12, 2019 release, Table 1)
datasets.size: 2,508 total hours, 2,019 validated hours, 58,250 voices, 29 released languages (38 collecting)
datasets.preprocessing: mono 16-bit MP3, 48 kHz; only clips with 2 first up-votes are valid; repeated sentences removed from train/dev/test

datasets.name: Common Voice internal Feb 2019 version, 10 languages (Table 2)
datasets.size: e.g. German 65,745 train / 7,982 dev / 7,897 test clips; Slovenian 728 / 110 / 213
datasets.split: as close as possible to 80% train, 10% dev, 10% test; one speaker in one split only
datasets.source: internal multilingual version of Common Voice, Feb 2019
datasets.preprocessing: splits do not match official releases

models.name: Mozilla DeepSpeech v0.3.0
models.architecture: 6-layer unidirectional CTC model: 3 fully connected, 1 LSTM, 2 fully connected
models.init_from: pre-trained English DeepSpeech (0 to 5 layers copied; none = from scratch)
models.context: 19 spliced frames (9 past + 1 + 9 future) x 26 MFCC = 494-dim input

training.regularisation: early stopping on dev loss: triggers if dev loss rises over 5 sequential epochs, or fails to improve by more than mean loss threshold 0.5 over 5 epochs with window std < 0.5

other.Adam other hyperparameters: deferred to DeepSpeech v0.3.0 source, not in paper

inference.samples: one run per language and layer setting; no seeds reported

metrics.name: Character Error Rate (CER)
metrics.definition: Levenshtein distance of characters between ground-truth transcript and decoding result, on test set

baselines: DeepSpeech trained from scratch on target-language data (0 layers copied)
eval.protocol: Test-set CER per language for 0-5 transferred layers; improvement averaged over 12 languages with std (Fig 5). No significance test, single run.

availability.code: CorporaCreator (bucketing) and common-voice-wiki-scraper on GitHub; DeepSpeech v0.3.0

evidence.quote: We report Character Error Rate as opposed to Word Error

results.claim: Corpus scale: hours collected across languages and participants.
results.quote: Over 50,000 individuals have participated so far, resulting in 2,500 hours of collected audio.

results.claim: Mean CER improvement from English transfer across 12 target languages.
results.setup: DeepSpeech v0.3.0, transfer from English, 12 languages, best layer count (abstract); Feb 2019 internal splits
results.quote: we ﬁnd an average Character Error Rate improvement of 5.99 ± 5.48 for twelve target
results.note: The std is almost as large as the mean; the abstract does not say which layer count.

results.claim: Copying four layers from English gave the best final model on most languages.
results.quote: we observe a trend in which four layers copied from pre-trained En-

results.setup: Chuvash (1,023 train clips, 5 train speakers), 4 layers copied vs none
results.table: Table 3, row cv, column 4 (27.21) versus column None (48.1)

results.claim: Slovenian CER with 4 layers versus scratch.
results.setup: Slovenian (728 train clips), 4 layers vs none
results.table: Table 3, row sl, column 4 (15.35) versus column None (23.35)

results.claim: Transfer gives almost no gain for German, the largest language.
results.setup: German (65,745 train clips), best (3 layers) vs scratch
results.table: Table 3, row de, column 3 (43.60) versus column None (43.76)
results.note: German and French CER stays about 43 for all layer counts; unexplained in paper

results.claim: Test and dev set sizes chosen for 99% confidence and 1% margin of error relative to training set size.
results.note: Paper states: confidence level of 99% with a margin of error of 1% relative to the number of clips in the training set.

results.claim: Splits are speaker-disjoint so train speakers are not seen at test time, which would skew results.

limits: CER chosen over WER as more language-agnostic; WER can be misleading for languages without whitespace words (footnote 12).
Experiments use an internal Feb 2019 version, and splits do not match official releases.
Some train sets have very few speakers (e.g. Tatar 3, Slovenian 3), a hard speaker-generalisation case.
Single run per setting, no seeds or significance tests; large std in the headline gain.
Only DeepSpeech v0.3.0 (2014 style) and CER; no WER, no noise/accent or demographic breakdown, no language-model decoding stated.
Validation is crowdsourced with 2 votes; early voting bugs gave clips with more than 3 votes (majority rule).
Prompts are read speech, not spontaneous.
Table 1 italic (unreleased) data is not distinguishable in the text extraction.
